lesson.title: Decades and Octaves: Measuring How Fast a Filter Cuts
lesson.summary: Roll-off rate measures how quickly a filter's attenuation increases as frequency moves into the stopband, conventionally stated in decibels per decade or decibels per octave, and it is set entirely by the filter's order.
lesson.body:
Roll-off rate answers the question: once you are past the edge of the passband, how fast does the filter's attenuation actually increase as frequency continues to move away? You already have the answer in terms of decades from Filter Order: an order-n filter rolls off at approximately 20n dB per decade, where a decade means any tenfold change in frequency, so the rate is the same whether you are looking at the region from 1 kHz to 10 kHz or from 10 kHz to 100 kHz.

Engineers just as often describe roll-off in decibels per octave, where an octave is a doubling of frequency rather than a tenfold increase, borrowed from music where doubling frequency is one octave higher. Because a decade and an octave are different-sized steps, converting between the two rates requires knowing how many octaves fit inside one decade: since 2 to the x equals 10 when x = log2(10), about 3.322, one decade equals about 3.322 octaves.

Convert the two roll-off rates you already calculated. A first-order filter's 20 dB per decade becomes 20 divided by 3.322, about 6.02 dB per octave, which is the origin of the common shorthand six dB per octave for a single-pole filter. A second-order filter's 40 dB per decade becomes 40 divided by 3.322, about 12.04 dB per octave, the source of the equally common twelve dB per octave figure used for two-pole filters, such as those in loudspeaker crossover networks.

Roll-off rate matters directly for Bandwidth: a filter with a steep roll-off can sit close to an interfering frequency and still adequately suppress it, while a shallow, first-order roll-off needs much more frequency separation, effectively a wider guard band, to achieve the same suppression. This is exactly why designers reach for higher-order filters, at the cost of extra components, when two signals of interest sit close together in frequency.
